clinicalPearls: Presents with progressive loss of central acuity, marked photophobia (day blindness or hemeralopia) and acquired dyschromatopsia, usually with preserved night vision
Fundus may be normal early, later showing a bull's-eye maculopathy or granular macular atrophy with temporal disc pallor
Photopic electroretinographic responses and flicker responses are reduced or absent while scotopic rod responses remain normal, which is the key distinction from cone-rod dystrophy
Inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive or X-linked, with genes such as GUCA1A, GUCY2D, PDE6C and RPGR implicated
By definition rods are spared functionally, so significant peripheral field loss and nyctalopia should raise suspicion of an evolving cone-rod pattern
Colour vision testing shows a generalised disturbance rather than a single congenital axis defect
Care is supportive with tinted or edge-filter lenses for photophobia, refractive correction, low-vision support and genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Progressive cone dystrophy is an inherited degeneration confined largely to the cone photoreceptor system. Defects in genes controlling cone phototransduction and guanylate cyclase signalling (for example GUCA1A, GUCY2D, PDE6C) disturb the recovery phase of the cone light response and lead to progressive cone dysfunction and cell death. Because rod photoreceptors are relatively preserved, patients retain night vision while losing central acuity, colour discrimination and photopic sensitivity. Over years some cases develop rod involvement and reclassify as cone-rod dystrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Cone-rod dystrophy once rod involvement appears
Stationary cone dysfunction syndromes such as achromatopsia and blue cone monochromacy
Occult macular dystrophy with a normal fundus
additionalInvestigations: Photopic and flicker full-field electroretinography showing reduced cone responses with preserved rod responses
Multifocal electroretinography to localise central cone loss
Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography for foveal outer retinal atrophy
Fundus autofluorescence for bull's-eye or central abnormal signal
Formal colour vision assessment showing generalised dyschromatopsia
Molecular genetic testing to identify the causative gene
redFlags: Onset of night blindness or peripheral constriction suggesting progression to cone-rod dystrophy
Severe disabling photophobia limiting daily function
Rapid deterioration of acuity warranting prompt electrophysiology and genetics
Positive family history indicating relatives who should be screened and counselled
reference.prognosis: Central vision declines slowly but progressively over years, and most patients reach the low-vision range; the tempo and endpoint depend on the underlying genotype.
pitfalls: Confusing a progressive cone dystrophy with a stationary cone dysfunction syndrome by not documenting deterioration over time
Missing early disease when the fundus still appears normal by omitting electrophysiology
Overlooking evolution into cone-rod dystrophy when night vision begins to fail
Interpreting acquired dyschromatopsia as a congenital colour defect
management: Provide low-vision rehabilitation with magnifiers, high-contrast and adaptive aids, since no disease-modifying therapy currently exists
Manage disabling photophobia with tinted and photochromic lenses and advise ultraviolet protection
Correct refractive error and optimise residual central acuity
Offer molecular genetic testing and genetic counselling, and consider referral to gene-directed therapy trials where relevant
Follow up regularly to detect evolution to a cone-rod pattern with peripheral field loss and night blindness
Arrange certification of visual impairment and educational, occupational and social support
Screen and counsel family members according to the inheritance pattern identified
